docs.abstract: Cardinal Joachim Meisner, the archbishop of Cologne whose conservative positions found him apologizing more than once during the years that he led Germany’s largest and wealthiest diocese, has retired, the archdiocese said Friday.
docs.snippet: Cardinal Joachim Meisner, the archbishop of Cologne whose conservative positions found him apologizing more than once during the years that he led Germany’s largest and wealthiest diocese, has retired, the archdiocese said Friday.
docs.lead_paragraph: Cardinal Joachim Meisner, the archbishop of Cologne whose conservative positions found him apologizing more than once during the years that he led Germany’s largest and wealthiest diocese, has retired, the archdiocese said Friday. Pope Francis accepted Cardinal Meisner’s request to retire, the archdiocese said in a statement. The cardinal, 80, had offered to step down after his 75th birthday but was asked by Pope Benedict XVI to stay on. After he was named to the position in 1988 by Pope John Paul II, he became known for his provocative statements, including comparing abortion to the Holocaust and using the Nazi’s term for the modernist artworks they despised — “degenerate” — to describe art with no religious connection. But he earned respect for refusing to bow to political pressure from Communist-era leaders while he was the leader of the Roman Catholic Church in Berlin and East Germany from 1980 to 1988.

headline.main: Archbishop of Cologne, Germany’s Largest Diocese, Retires
headline.print_headline: Germany: Cologne’s Archbishop Retires

docs.abstract: The United States’ top representative to the Syrian opposition, Robert S. Ford, retired from the Foreign Service on Friday, the State Department said.

docs.lead_paragraph: The United States’ top representative to the Syrian opposition, Robert S. Ford, retired from the Foreign Service on Friday, the State Department said. Lawrence Silverman, the acting deputy assistant secretary for Near Eastern affairs, will serve as his replacement until a successor is chosen. State Department officials said this month that Mr. Ford was expected to retire soon. As the American ambassador to Syria, Mr. Ford played an active role in challenging President Bashar al-Assad’s crackdown on the political opposition. In February 2012, as the security situation in Syria worsened, the American Embassy was closed. Mr. Ford later became the chief American envoy to the moderate Syrian opposition. Mr. Ford played a central role during the first two rounds of the peace talks in Geneva.

docs.lead_paragraph: President Mahinda Rajapaksa on Friday rejected calls for an international investigation into accusations of massacres and human rights violations during the final phase of Sri Lanka’s civil war, which ended in 2009. “If there is evidence, let them show us,” Mr. Rajapaksa said. “We will look into it.” Meeting with an association of foreign journalists in Sri Lanka for the first time in three years, Mr. Rajapaksa said that recent resolutions criticizing Sri Lanka at the United Nations Human Rights Council could arise from a hidden agenda. On Thursday, the State Department released a report that was highly critical of the Rajapaksa government, claiming that in 2013 “attacks, harassment, and threats by pro-government loyalists against critics of the government were prevalent, contributed to widespread self-censorship by journalists, and diminished democratic activity.” On Friday, Mr. Rajapaksa likened the friction between the United States and Sri Lanka to “Cassius Clay fighting with a schoolboy,” a reference to the boxer now known as Muhammad Ali. But he said that the two countries were still friends.

docs.lead_paragraph: BRUSSELS — IN early 2009, as many as 40,000 civilians were killed in the final days of Sri Lanka’s civil war, having been herded into an area about the size of Central Park and subjected to relentless shelling. No one has been held accountable for these crimes, and even now the government in Colombo remains intent on burying the past. Only an international commission of inquiry stands any chance of rectifying this omission. So when the United Nations Human Rights Council meets Monday in Geneva, it should seek an investigation. It would be a decisive step toward justice and reconciliation in Sri Lanka.

headline.main: Let the U.N. Unmask the Criminals of Sri Lanka’s War
headline.print_headline: Let the U.N. Unmask the Criminals of Sri Lanka’s War

(Showtime) THE IMPOSSIBLE (2012) Naomi Watts received an Oscar nomination for her role as Maria, an Englishwoman living in Japan, who is spending Christmas 2004 with her husband (Ewan McGregor) and three sons at a luxurious beach resort in Thailand when the tsunami hits. Maria is washed inland with her oldest son (Tom Holland, above, with Ms. Watts), leaving her badly injured and unable to find the rest of her family. “Survivors are also witnesses, and ‘The Impossible’ shows us, through the eyes of one unbelievably lucky family, some terrible things, including mangled bodies and parents in despair,” A. O. Scott wrote in The New York Times of this second feature from the Spanish director Juan Antonio Bayona, based on a real-life account, which uses digital imagery, sound design and editing techniques to recreate both the violence and desolation that resulted from the natural disaster. “But there is a troubling complacency and a lack of compassion in ‘The Impossible,’ which is less an examination of mass destruction than the tale of a spoiled holiday. docs.abstract: Chest hair, that 1970s signifier of strength and virility, isn’t the sex symbol that it once was.
docs.snippet: Chest hair, that 1970s signifier of strength and virility, isn’t the sex symbol that it once was.
docs.lead_paragraph: Chest hair, that 1970s signifier of strength and virility, isn’t the sex symbol that it once was — especially in this youth-obsessed era, when even alpha males are as waxed as a figurine. Ingrid Berthon-Moine plumbs deeper into the matter with “V,” her photo series of hirsute men. The images are cropped so tightly that they resemble female pubic hair. “By using humor, you make a connection,” says the 36-year-old French artist, who has explored — and upended — other beauty and gender tropes, including the masochistic nature of pedicures (in one of her short films she took a cheese grater to her heels) and the male ideal (satirized in a photography project that centered on the anatomy of Greek classical statues). Berthon-Moine knows her work isn’t for everyone. “You have to accept that people will like it or hate it and that is fine,” she says. “Art will not change the world but it can shift the way we look at it.”

docs.abstract: Just in time for “Gravity”‘s big Oscar moment, a thread of retro-futurism is running through the fall/winter women’s collections.

docs.lead_paragraph: Will “Gravity” get the Oscar for best picture? We’ll have to wait till Sunday to find out — but the fashion world seems to have deemed it a winner, if the astronaut-inspired clothing hitting the runway this season is any evidence. This microtrend hit the catwalk like a rocket at one of the first runway shows in New York: Organic by John Patrick. The designer riffed on the NASA suit with quilted metallic Ts, silver pants and mod boots reminiscent of ’60s space age fashion. Flash forward to Paris, where the designer Gareth Pugh presented a collection of cloudlike white dresses and mirrored silver trousers and tops that sculpted the body like futuristic armor. Finally, at Rick Owens, where the clothing always looks as if it is from the future, the designer showed white quilted motocross pants and high-necked zip-front jackets that winked at Hollywood’s interpretation of space-ship uniforms.

docs.lead_paragraph: This story about top tech firms agreeing not to compete for workers is really amazing. docs.abstract: The Broad Street brogue — soda is sewda, house is hay-ouse — is sadly absent in the movies.
docs.snippet: The Broad Street brogue — soda is sewda, house is hay-ouse — is sadly absent in the movies.
docs.lead_paragraph: THE Philadelphia regional accent remains arguably the most distinctive, and least imitable, accent in North America. Let’s not argue about this. Ask anyone to do a Lawn Guyland accent or a charming Southern drawl and that person will approximate it. Same goes for a Texas twang or New Orleans yat, a Valley Girl totally omigod. Philly-South Jersey patois is a bit harder: No vowel escapes diphthongery, no hard consonant is safe from a mid-palate dent. Extra syllables pile up so as to avoid inconvenient tongue contact or mouth closure. If you forget to listen closely, the Philadelphia, or Filelfia, accent may sound like mumbled Mandarin without the tonal shifts.

headline.main: The Sound of Philadelphia Fades Out

The countdown begins at 1:30 on E!; at 5 on the TV Guide Channel; and at 6 on Channel 11. Red-carpet coverage begins at 7 on ABC. Postshow coverage follows at 11:30 on E! docs.abstract: In “Five Came Back,” Mark Harris, an Entertainment Weekly columnist, examines the wartime lives and work of John Huston, Frank Capra, John Ford, George Stevens and William Wyler.
docs.snippet: In “Five Came Back,” Mark Harris, an Entertainment Weekly columnist, examines the wartime lives and work of John Huston, Frank Capra, John Ford, George Stevens and William Wyler.
docs.lead_paragraph: Mark Harris, a columnist at Entertainment Weekly and the author of the marvelous “Pictures at a Revolution: Five Movies and the Birth of the New Hollywood,” from 2008, bets again on his lucky number for an excursion into a very different motion picture revolution. “Five Came Back,” modestly subtitled “A Story of Hollywood and the Second World War,” is a tough-minded, information-packed and irresistibly readable work of movie-minded cultural criticism. Like the best World War II films, it highlights marquee names in a familiar plot to explore some serious issues: the human cost of military service, the hypnotic power of cinema and the tension between artistic integrity and the exigencies of war. Mr. Harris shows how — more than Technicolor, CinemaScope or even the collapse of the Production Code — World War II changed the way Americans looked at the movies.

headline.main: Cameras Shooting in Battle: Five Auteurs and Their World War II Films

docs.abstract: Gay rights held Hollywood’s attention at the Oscars, but Ellen DeGeneres, the host, was more lighthearted about the issue.
docs.snippet: Gay rights held Hollywood’s attention at the Oscars, but Ellen DeGeneres, the host, was more lighthearted about the issue.
docs.lead_paragraph: “12 Years a Slave” won best picture, but for much of the evening, it was gay rights, not race, that held Hollywood’s attention at the Oscars. Jared Leto dragged the real world into Sunday night’s celebration of make-believe. After winning the best supporting actor for portraying a transgender AIDS patient in “Dallas Buyers Club,” Mr. Leto voiced support for protesters in Ukraine and Venezuela. He championed gay people. “To those of you out there who have ever felt injustice because of who you are or who you love, tonight, I stand here in front of the world with you and for you.” Hollywood is so righteous, suddenly, about gay rights, and that’s a little puzzling because for so long, movies were part of the problem. Professional basketball has its first openly gay player, Jason Collins, but it’s still hard to think of romantic leads — male or female — who are A-list Hollywood movie stars and also openly gay.

headline.main: Staking a Claim on Social Causes
headline.print_headline: Staking a Claim on Social Causes

docs.snippet: A sweet mixture of winter vegetables that works on its own as a side or as part of a few different kinds of main dishes.
docs.lead_paragraph: This is a sweet mixture of comforting winter vegetables that you can serve on its own as a side dish, or use as the component of a polenta, big bowl, frittata or omelet, or pasta. I roast the squash in one pan and the other vegetables together in another. If you have a small oven, roast the squash first, then the other vegetables. Or you can use two shelves and switch the trays top to bottom halfway through the roasting.

headline.main: Roasted Winter Vegetable Medley

docs.abstract: A comforting main dish that combines savory oven-baked polenta with sweet oven-roasted root vegetables.
docs.snippet: A comforting main dish that combines savory oven-baked polenta with sweet oven-roasted root vegetables.
docs.lead_paragraph: In this comforting, perfect winter dinner I roast the vegetables and make the polenta in the oven at the same time. To accommodate the temperature requirements of each element of the dish, I use a slightly higher temperature than I usually use for polenta and I roast the vegetables at a lower temperature for longer. I top the polenta with a ladleful of marinara sauce, and spoon the vegetables on top. You could serve the polenta with only the roasted vegetables as well, so I have made the marinara sauce optional.

headline.main: Roasted Root Vegetables With Polenta

He has arrived in Laurel with a one-year student visa and is introduced to a social worker named Helen, who is supposed to be “his chaperone into Middle America — his personal tour guide of our town’s shopping malls, grocery stores, banks and bureaucracies.”

docs.abstract: In a new puppet play, “Hobo Grunt Cycle,” the political is personal.
docs.snippet: In a new puppet play, “Hobo Grunt Cycle,” the political is personal.
docs.lead_paragraph: Political puppet theater, of the Bread and Puppet variety, is by its nature not very subtle. What packs a surprising punch out on the street can often feel like getting hammered with the pious and the obvious in a stage setting. That’s a major drawback of “Hobo Grunt Cycle,” a work by the Lone Wolf Tribe founder Kevin Augustine at Dixon Place through March 15, which marries extraordinary life-size puppets and Chaplinesque antics to show how we use soldiers, fighting pit bulls and clowns for our own various gratifications, then kick them to the curb, wounded and forgotten. Augustine, who possesses formidable puppet-making and pantomime talents, is our main hobo clown — a genre, we learn, at the bottom of the clown “chain of command,” well below patrician whiteface and the middle-rank, red-nosed “Auguste.” He is not only forced to become a military fighting machine, trained to shoot and bayonet to kill (the work employs considerable World War I imagery), he also tenderly nurses a badly injured pit bull, another creature raised to fight on command, and even helps a delicate little (puppet) bird convalesce. Amid all this arrive a few theatrically unbearable moments. At one point, we hear two parents, on the other side of a locked door, as they wail for their (puppet) war-vet son, an amputee and PTSD sufferer, who has apparently killed himself in his bedroom. It’s just too much.

headline.main: After Hours | Tears of a Clown

Japan and North Korea do not have formal diplomatic ties and have not held government-to-government talks since late 2012. The diplomats met for two hours in the Chinese city of Shenyang on the sidelines of talks between the Red Cross societies of both nations to discuss the return of the remains of Japanese who died in Korea at the end of World War II. docs.abstract: The implications of Vladimir Putin’s Crimean adventure.
docs.snippet: The implications of Vladimir Putin’s Crimean adventure.
docs.lead_paragraph: 1) It probably wasn’t rhetorically helpful, but John Kerry was entirely correct when he called Vladimir Putin’s quasi-invasion of Ukraine the work of “somebody who is acting out of weakness.” Putin’s aggression doesn’t undermine anything I wrote a week ago about the limits of Russian power and the essential implausibility of the Kremlin’s grand ambitions; this gambit is a salvage operation following a major political setback, not a plausible stepping-stone toward some sweeping long-term objective. The echoes of earlier Russian aggressions are real, but the comparison to Czechoslovakia in 1968 and Hungary in 1956 should be illuminating: In those cases, Russia was projecting power well beyond its borders, and using force to keep a relatively-vast sphere of influence intact, whereas in this case it’s projecting power … in the Russian-speaking regions of a former Soviet republic/czarist province. You can make the case that Putin is playing as well as he can with a losing hand, or you can make the case that he’s out of touch with reality and stumbling into an epic disaster. But either way, what we’re witnessing isn’t the re-emergence of Russia as a major geopolitical threat to the United States and our allies, unless by “major geopolitical threat” you mean “weakened ex-empire struggling to control its own periphery.”

headline.main: Five Theses on Ukraine

docs.abstract: Hollywood makes going to extremes to maintain even the false illusion of a youthful face seem natural. Do some parts of the country push us to similar extremes when it comes to raising families?

docs.lead_paragraph: It has been hard for Oscar watchers to let go of the sight of Kim Novak, puffed and padded into a pseudo-youthful effigy of an 81-year-old woman. As Amanda Hess wrote on Slate’s XXFactor blog, Hollywood is a “horrible” place to be an old woman. It’s not just Hollywood — a few years ago, Dominique Browning wrote of her cohort: “We’ve reached a stage where cosmetic surgery is so readily available that in certain circles it is expected of women and men to avail themselves of these age-deniers. If you choose not to partake of the benefits of needle and knife, you are judged to be making a statement. You are taking a position against the current standards of beauty.”

headline.main: It’s Harder to Age in Hollywood. Where Is It Harder to Raise Kids?

docs.snippet: This film creates a piece of social and sexual history by reshooting segments of the 1980 film “Cruising” that were lost after being cut.
docs.lead_paragraph: The man in the black leather vest looks nervous. All around him, glistening half-naked men dance to the disco beat as smoke curls in the air. They writhe, touch and kiss, skin against skin, leather against leather. A guy in chaps pauses and locks his eyes on our nervous man. Here, looking is cruising, an overt exchange of desire: It’s about watching and waiting, and being conspicuously out of the closet and the thrilling promise of something more. Then the scene stops and the actors wait as James Franco and Travis Mathews, the directors choreographing this bacchanalia, plot their next move.

docs.lead_paragraph: The State House of Representatives on Tuesday approved a measure that would allow state health department officials to conduct unannounced inspections of abortion clinics. The clinic inspections now require warrants, and Democrats argued that the legislation would empower public officials to harass abortion providers. Republicans said the bill would ensure that abortion providers were following state and federal laws. The bill was approved on a nearly party-line vote, with one Republican voting against and one Democrat voting in favor. The measure heads to the Senate, where it has strong support from the Republican majority. The bill was drafted by the Center for Arizona Policy, a Christian organization that championed a recent bill that would have allowed business owners to cite religious beliefs in refusing to conduct business with gays and others. Gov. Jan Brewer, a Republican, vetoed that bill.

headline.main: Arizona: Bill Advances to Allow Surprise Inspections of Abortion Clinics

Cunha, found that a chemist who may have compromised tens of thousands of criminal cases was the “sole bad actor” at the drug laboratory where she worked, but took its management to task for lapses that it said had created an atmosphere that enabled her actions. The chemist, Annie Dookhan, admitted last fall that she falsified test results at the Hinton State Laboratory Institute in Boston, and is serving up to five years in prison. The laboratory has since closed. Mr. Cunha’s report, which was made public on Tuesday, said that the laboratory lacked important protocols and adequate oversight and that investigators were retesting drug samples in more than 2,000 additional cases.

docs.lead_paragraph: Florence Nightingale and Clara Barton, two great heroines of 19th-century nursing, were born a year apart but in utterly different circumstances. Nightingale was born in the spring of 1820 to a wealthy British family living in Italy. They returned to England shortly after, entertaining the beau monde of the day at Embley Park, their estate near London. Barton, born on Christmas Day in 1821, was the youngest of five children in a farming family in North Oxford, Mass. Her mother and sister Dolly seem to have suffered from mental illness; Clara was raised, in large part, by her brother Davie. She became a teacher at the age of 15.

docs.abstract: More than 25 years after arriving in Managua during the Sandinista-contra conflict, the author returns, finding contrasts between her memories and today’s Nicaragua.
docs.snippet: More than 25 years after arriving in Managua during the Sandinista-contra conflict, the author returns, finding contrasts between her memories and today’s Nicaragua.
docs.lead_paragraph: Managua’s airport doesn’t look anything like it did the day I first arrived there with an ill-considered buzz cut, two donated microscopes and a mind brimming with untested idealism. That was in 1985, when the Sandinista revolution and the American-backed contra campaign opposing it were in full swing. I had taken a leave from college to see the revolution up close, to lend my hand in whatever way I could, including teaching, and ended up staying for nearly three years. At the immigration counter, a compañero in fatigues insisted, in Spanish, that I redo my forms. Leafing through my American passport, he noted that I was born in Germany, but he seemed disappointed that my birthplace was in the western half of the country, not in socialist East Germany. To tell the truth, I was a little disappointed, too, and all the more so when my microscopes, destined for a rural health clinic, were seized by customs.

headline.main: Revisiting Nicaragua, This Time as a Tourist
headline.print_headline: Revisiting the Revolution, This Time as a Tourist

docs.lead_paragraph: GRAND PORTAGE, Minn. — For moose, this year’s winter-long deep freeze across the Upper Midwest is truly ideal weather. The large, gangly creatures are adapted to deep snow: Their hollow fur insulates them like fiberglass does in a house. And the prolonged cold helps eradicate pests that prey on moose, like ticks and meningeal worm, or brain worm. Yet moose in Minnesota are dying at an alarming rate, and biologists are perplexed as to why.

docs.lead_paragraph: In fiercely competitive world of tech start-ups, the idea of a website devoted to doing things out of the kindness of one’s heart may seem counterintuitive. But that’s just what the 26-year-old British model, actress and Cambridge graduate Lily Cole has put forth with her new online social platform and app, Impossible. The site, which debuted last year in the U.K. but launches stateside this month, functions as a real-life, high-tech giving tree of sorts. Users can post their wishes — for goods or services, for skills like learning to play the piano or for loftier goals like curing disease or ending prejudice — and grant those of others. Once a wish is granted, users post thank-you notes, taking the site’s warm-and-fuzzy factor even further.

docs.lead_paragraph: The Norman Bird Sanctuary is 325 acres of startling geography overlooking the Atlantic Ocean and the Sakonnet River in Middletown, R.I. Its benefactor was Mabel Norman Cerio, a local artist who lived in its farmhouse in the late 19th century and bequeathed the property “for the propagation, preservation and protection of birds.” Since 1949, the sanctuary has done just that, but Ms. Cerio’s 18th-century house has been slowly rotting away. In a collaboration between the Urban Design Group of Bristol, R.I., and Foster Associates of Portsmouth, R.I., the place was taken down to its studs and meticulously reconstructed. It’s spare, though not spartan, so the emphasis is on the architectural details and the views. The farmhouse has seven bedrooms and sleeps 16 (there are three bunk beds in one bedroom); it is open for retreats of all sorts, from family weekend “roosts” to yoga retreats. Natasha Harrison, executive director of the Norman Bird Sanctuary, said that next year she hopes to host artists’ residencies, too. Information: 401-846-2577 or normanbirdsanctuary.org.

docs.lead_paragraph: In 1995, Maggie Keswick, an expert on Chinese gardens who was terminally ill with breast cancer, founded an organization with her husband, the architecture critic Charles Jencks, to provide free information and support for people with cancer and their families. The first Maggie’s Centre opened in Edinburgh in November 1996, a year after her death, with services that included guidance in navigating the medical system and advice on where to buy a wig. Now there are 16 centers in Britain and one in Hong Kong. All are on the grounds of cancer hospitals, and share a reliance on design to promote healing and comfort. “Architecture amplifies the message,” Mr. Jencks said. “Maggie’s Centres: A Blueprint for Cancer Care,” on view from Friday through April 25 at the New York School of Interior Design, features centers designed by Frank Gehry (in Dundee), Rem Koolhaas, Richard Rogers, Steven Holl, and Piers Gough with Paul Smith. Information: 212-472-1500 or nysid.edu.

docs.lead_paragraph: Public contact between the representatives of the Taliban and Pakistani government resumed on Wednesday as Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif made another push to put a wavering peace dialogue back on track. Mr. Sharif has invited a team of Taliban representatives to his official residence in Islamabad on Thursday, according to government officials. Maulana Sami ul-Haq, a religious leader who represents the Taliban, said he has accepted the invitation and would discuss ways to carry the peace talks forward. Earlier, committees representing the government and the Taliban met at Mr. Haq’s seminary in northwestern town Akora Khattak, the first such meeting since Feb.17, when talks were suspended after a faction of the Taliban claimed responsibility for the killing of 23 paramilitary soldiers. Despite a Taliban announcement of a cease-fire, terrorist attacks have continued across the country in recent days and have been claimed by obscure militant groups. The latest attack occurred Wednesday in northwestern Hangu district where a roadside bomb killed six paramilitary soldiers and wounded eight others.

headline.main: Pakistan’s Talks With Taliban Resume

docs.abstract: A French convert to Islam was convicted of using the Internet to disseminate terrorist propaganda and promote participation in terrorist acts and was sentenced by a Paris court to one year in prison and two more on probation late Tuesday.
docs.snippet: A French convert to Islam was convicted of using the Internet to disseminate terrorist propaganda and promote participation in terrorist acts and was sentenced by a Paris court to one year in prison and two more on probation late Tuesday.
docs.lead_paragraph: A French convert to Islam was convicted of using the Internet to disseminate terrorist propaganda and promote participation in terrorist acts and was sentenced by a Paris court to one year in prison and two more on probation late Tuesday. The case is the first using a law passed in 2012 that makes “cyber jihad” a crime and potentially has serious consequences for freedom of expression in France. The law was passed in response to the attacks in Toulouse by Mohammed Merah, who killed seven people including three children and apparently was inspired in part by extremist Internet postings. The maximum sentence in Tuesday’s case could have been five years in prison, and the relatively light term given to Romain Letellier, 27, suggested that both prosecutors and judges were still considering how to apply the new law. The prosecutor said that the trial was happening in a context where young people become radicalized rapidly after reading material on the Internet.

headline.main: Jail Sentence in France Over ‘Cyber Jihad’

docs.abstract: How the College Board revolutionized the most controversial exam in America.
docs.snippet: How the College Board revolutionized the most controversial exam in America.
docs.lead_paragraph: In July 2012, a few months before he was to officially take over as president of the College Board, David Coleman invited Les Perelman, then a director of writing at M.I.T., to come meet with him in Lower Manhattan. Of the many things the College Board does — take part in research, develop education policy, create curriculums — it is perhaps most recognized as the organization that administers the SAT, and Perelman was one of the exam’s harshest and most relentless critics. Since 2005, when the College Board added an essay to the SAT (raising the total possible score from 1,600 to 2,400), Perelman had been conducting research that highlighted what he believed were the inherent absurdities in how the essay questions were formulated and scored. His earliest findings showed that length, more than any other factor, correlated with a high score on the essay. More recently, Perelman coached 16 students who were retaking the test after having received mediocre scores on the essay section. He told them that details mattered but factual accuracy didn’t. “You can tell them the War of 1812 began in 1945,” he said. He encouraged them to sprinkle in little-used but fancy words like “plethora” or “myriad” and to use two or three preselected quotes from prominent figures like Franklin Delano Roosevelt, regardless of whether they were relevant to the question asked. Fifteen of his pupils scored higher than the 90th percentile on the essay when they retook the exam, he said.

headline.main: The Story Behind the SAT Overhaul
headline.print_headline: The SAT is Hated by . . . All of the Above

docs.lead_paragraph: It’s a tough choice, but if I had to pick the most Wes Anderson moment in “The Grand Budapest Hotel,” it would be the part when inmates escape from a prison using tiny sledgehammers and pickaxes that have been smuggled past the guards inside fancy frosted pastries. docs.lead_paragraph: Raleigh has traditionally been lumped with Durham and Chapel Hill as part of the Research Triangle — the land of science, technology and, in the run-up to this month’s N.C.A.A. tournament, college basketball. Today, North Carolina’s capital is awash in entrepreneurial energy from homegrown clothing labels and converted art galleries to craft breweries and ambitious restaurants. More than merely one of the Triangle’s three vertexes, Raleigh is now defining itself as a destination worth exploring on its own merits, regardless of what lies beyond the city limits.

Rockefeller was eventually unmasked as Christian Gerhartsreiter, and in 2013 was convicted of a murder that had occurred nearly 30 years earlier. He confessed to Kirn that the inspiration for his alter ego came from “The Great Gatsby.” “Surprisingly, he told me he didn’t identify with the character of Gatsby so much as he did with Nick, the narrator,” Kirn said in an email interview. “I think he was lying about this. I think he knew that I, like Nick, and like Fitzgerald, had grown up in Minnesota; he wanted to get in good with me by creating a sense of having something in common.”

docs.lead_paragraph: The State Legislature passed a bill on Thursday prohibiting “upskirting,” or secretly photographing up someone’s clothing in public without his or her consent. The move came one day after the state’s highest court ruled that an existing law prohibiting secret photographing of nude or partly nude people did not apply to the case of Michael Robertson — who was arrested in 2010 and accused of using his cellphone to take images of women’s crotch areas on Boston’s public transit — because the women he photographed were dressed. The measure would make the secret photographing or videotaping of “sexual or intimate parts,” either naked or clothed, when a person could reasonably expect them not to be visible to the public, punishable by more than two years in prison and/or a $5,000 fine.

docs.lead_paragraph: The Constitutional Court on Thursday ruled in favor of a former army chief who was appealing the legality of his initial detention in 2012 in a case that resulted in his conviction and life sentence last year for plotting a coup against the government, according to a written statement posted on the court’s website. The ruling, which said that the rights of the former officer, Gen. Ilker Basbug, who served as military chief of staff from 2008 to 2010, had been violated, paved the way for his possible release from an Istanbul prison. The Constitutional Court said the lower court that held the five-year trial failed to publish its detailed reasoning for its verdict and send it to the appeals court, obstructing the defendant’s right to an appeal and violating a constitutional clause concerning personal freedom. The ruling could also be used as a precedent for the release of many of the more than 270 defendants who spent several years in prison before their convictions last year in the case known as the Ergenekon affair. The government’s prosecution of that case was seen as an effort to curb the role of Turkey’s military in politics, but it was also criticized for ensnaring people who were opponents of the government, including politicians, academics, journalists and writers.

headline.main: Turkish Court Backs General’s Appeal

(TCM) FRIDAY NIGHT SPOTLIGHT: FOOD IN THE MOVIES A visual feast begins with “Eat Drink Man Woman” (1994), above, Ang Lee’s Oscar-nominated drama for best foreign-language film about a father, Mr. Chu (Sihung Lung) — the greatest chef in Taipei — who has lost his joie de vivre, and his three beautiful star-crossed daughters (Chien-Lien Wu, Kuei-Mei-Yang and Yu-Wen Wang), who cannot escape his spell. Tensions are so high that at their extravagant Sunday dinners, the family can barely eat. And so he begins to supply spectacular lunches to the daughter of a family friend, who is too young to realize that his cooking is flawed: He has lost the use of his taste buds. “Wonderfully seductive, and nicely knowing about all of its characters’ appetites, ‘Eat Drink Man Woman’ makes for an uncomplicatedly pleasant experience,” Janet Maslin wrote in The New York Times. “This film’s use of food is both voluptuous and serious, amplifying the story even as it offers an irresistible diversion. The film succeeds in presenting Mr. Chu’s intricate cooking (rendered for the camera by three amazingly artful chefs) as an expression of larger traditionalism and as an endangered art.” Of the title, she added: “ ‘Food and sex,’ one character says succinctly, amplifying that four-ideogram phrase. ‘Basic human desires. Can’t avoid them.’ ” In “Mostly Martha” (2002), at 10:15, Martha (Martina Gedeck), a single, workaholic chef in Hamburg, Germany, finds her carefully organized life in disarray when she must care for her dead sister’s 8-year-old daughter (Maxime Foerste). Enter Mario, the Italian sous-chef (Sergio Castellitto) who can charm everyone but Martha. “The movie succeeds because the writer and director, Sandra Nettelbeck, seems as obsessive as her titular heroine,” Elvis Mitchell wrote in The Times. “The final confection is extremely enjoyable, though a few degrees shy of perfection.”

Before entering the American zone, he buried his gun and, while sheltering in an attic, hid letters from his new wife urging him in coded language to desert. During a home renovation in the 1980s, the bundle of letters was discovered, hidden in a wall, and returned to the doctor’s family. The correspondence revealed the trials of a young woman raising the three sons from her husband’s first marriage. That the soundtrack to her struggle was the whine of air-raid sirens and the thud of bombs made it all the more remarkable.

docs.abstract: Patrick Leigh Fermor’s European travel trilogy draws to a close.
docs.snippet: Patrick Leigh Fermor’s European travel trilogy draws to a close.
docs.lead_paragraph: In the winter of 1933, an 18-year-old named Patrick Leigh Fermor set out from the Hook of Holland to cross Europe on foot. His goal was Istanbul, which he bookishly insisted on calling Constantinople. He had little more in his rucksack than a volume of Horace and a few blank notebooks. He also had a bad reputation: The masters who expelled him from school — for a flirtation with a local girl — saw only “a dangerous mixture of sophistication and recklessness.” He spent the next year charming his way through a doomed prewar landscape of landed aristocrats, feudal peasants and benevolent monks, sleeping alternately in schlosses and hayricks. It was a journey that would become legendary, not so much for the extraordinary things he saw and recorded as for his prose — an utterly unique, hybrid vehicle that combines youthful exuberance with a dense, dauntingly erudite display of verbal artifice. Unlike most authors of travel literature (a rattlebag genre that doesn’t really do him justice) Leigh Fermor does not confine his role to that of camera obscura. He builds dense whorls of wordplay to echo the carvings in an old church door; he slips into baroque historical fantasias, scattering a shrapnel of words like “gabions,” “hydromel,” “eyot” and “swingle­trees” at the unsuspecting reader. In between salvos, there are moments of ferocious humor and quiet, lyrical beauty.

docs.lead_paragraph: The surf at Far Rockaway, Queens, is typically small, wind-tattered and weak, and for most of the year it’s freezing cold. Yes, there are days when the waves are passably good, and rare days when they are powerful and shapely, but that’s true of breaks in the Great Lakes and Italy. What sets Far Rockaway apart is that it’s a subway ride away from Manhattan, a fact recently rediscovered by a younger crop of culture workers who took up surfing and by dint of beginner’s zeal have added a wholesome, sun-spangled dimension to the hard-soled, mean-streets experience of life in New York, retrofitting Far Rockaway with smoothie stands and half-million-dollar surf shacks among the grim low-income high-rises.

docs.lead_paragraph: In June of this year, the World Cup in Brazil will begin not with a flashy musical number or a team of flying acrobats but with a simple scientific demonstration. A paralyzed teenager will make the ceremonial first kick. This feat will be accomplished through an “exoskeleton” directly controlled by the teenager’s thoughts and read through a helmet-mounted EEG machine. That kick, guided by an extraordinary brain-to-machine interface, may be our initiation into our post-human future. In that brave new world our memories will be recorded and swapped like old videotapes, self-aware robots will be our companions, and our consciousness, downloaded onto machines, will live forever. It’s a future Michio Kaku, the string theorist turned popular scientist, believes is inevitable and closer than we think.

docs.lead_paragraph: The Nabokov Code: Lorrie Moore’s new story collection, “Bark,” enters the hardcover fiction list at No. 13 — her third consecutive best seller, after the novel “A Gate at the Stairs” (2009) and the collection “Birds of America” (1998). Reviewing “Bark” on the cover of the Book Review a few weeks ago, David Gates noted that Moore shares Vladimir Nabokov’s affinity for obsessive wordplay, although her outlook is darker; she is, he wrote, “the most Beckettian of Nabokovians.” What Gates didn’t mention (but surely knew) was that “Bark” contains a direct tribute to Nabokov: Moore’s story “Referential,” about a couple visiting the woman’s son in a mental hospital, borrows its premise and some of its language from Nabokov’s 1948 story “Signs and Symbols,” in which the patient “imagines that everything happening around him is a veiled reference to his personality and existence.” A story about a story about a man who thinks everything is about him: How’s that for referential?

docs.lead_paragraph: In 1997, Rachel Kolberg was newly married, pregnant and living in Tel Aviv when she went to her first yoga class. It was a revelation. Her husband, Avraham, soon began practicing with her. “I was looking for some spiritual support,” he says. “Yoga gave that to me.” Seven years later, the couple opened their own studio, determined to introduce yoga to fellow Orthodox Jews in Beit Shemesh. They teach Iyengar yoga, a discipline that encourages the use of props to assist with poses. While yoga is increasingly popular in Israel, Avraham says, it is “revolutionary” in their neighborhood. Their students, taught in single-sex classes, are encouraged to come as they are, even in day clothes or long skirts, if necessary. The Kolbergs say yoga helps people who spend long days in prayer and study and aren’t physically active. But, Rachel says, “in our studio, we will never have practices that contradict our religion, such as mantras and chanting.” Julie Bosman

docs.lead_paragraph: On the night of Oct. 29, 2012, the basement storage of the Martha Graham Dance Company was overrun with water from the nearby Hudson River, pushed across the West Side Highway by Hurricane Sandy. docs.abstract: The venerable British stationer collaborated with Quentin Jones on an accessories line full of winking cats and graphic eyes.
docs.snippet: The venerable British stationer collaborated with Quentin Jones on an accessories line full of winking cats and graphic eyes.
docs.lead_paragraph: After being commissioned last fall by the British leather goods and stationery maker Smythson to make a series of collages for its London Fashion Week presentation, the mixed-media artist and filmmaker Quentin Jones is returning to the brand, this time applying her work directly onto the label’s signature stationery and accessories. The collaboration, available Monday at Colette in Paris and at smythson.com beginning March 31, features pouches, bags and notebooks from the brand’s Panama Legacy collection, designed by Rory O’Hanlon. These, together with coordinating keychains, bear the whimsical, surrealist illustrations and calligraphy that the 30-year-old Jones has become renowned for in the worlds of art and fashion. “I thought about my favorite examples of artists who work with pure lines: Miro, Picasso, early Hockney and Ben Nicholson,” says Jones of her approach to the visuals. Smythson’s classic Soho notebook has been rebelliously tagged in gold with the phrases “Soho Saint” and “Soho Sinner”; a winking cat adorns a zippered pouch and cross-body bag; a sharp white leather tote bears a cluster of floating eyes. And starting on March 31, the brand’s Panama notebooks can be custom-embossed with Jones’s motifs in Smythson’s New York store. “It is so fun for me to work in 3-D,” says Jones, “and to make things that I want to own and wear myself.”

headline.main: An It Artist Makes Her Mark on Smythson’s Storied Leather Goods

docs.lead_paragraph: A major goal of the recent redesign of NYTimes.com article pages was to improve page load speed and perceived performance. We focused on one of the more challenging sources of slow performance: third-party code, and, in particular, ads. Ads often load JavaScript files, which block the browser from loading other files until the script finishes executing. Combine that with the fact that ads are often placed near the top of the page and we have a recipe for a lot of blocked loading that will slow things down. By addressing the ad problem, we were able to make our new articles about 50 percent faster (these changes aren’t on the home page yet, but they will be soon).

headline.main: Stopping Ads From Slowing Down NYTimes.com

docs.lead_paragraph: The call of the red-winged blackbird announces spring while the snow still falls. His call — a powerful “conk-a-ree-e” — trails off and settles over the reeds, embodying the ancient promise that spring will return.

docs.lead_paragraph: We know you’re busy, but try to slow down for a moment. The city captured on this page by Jerome Liebling, who died in 2011, doesn’t reveal itself right away. Mr. Liebling, who became known as a member of the Photo League, a group of socially minded photographers that disbanded in 1951, dug deeply into his subjects, using still photography almost like film, to explore a condition rather than an instant. “He and his subjects are looking at each other,” said Rachel Liebling, who curated an exhibition of her father’s work, which is to run at the Steven Kasher Gallery from March 13 to April 19. “They’re looking at him and he’s looking at them. docs.abstract: Robert Smithson’s earthworks record the suburban landscape he was surrounded by as a boy in New Jersey.
docs.snippet: Robert Smithson’s earthworks record the suburban landscape he was surrounded by as a boy in New Jersey.
docs.lead_paragraph: In December 1967, Robert Smithson published a photographic essay in Artforum magazine that would become a landmark of 1960s art. Not only did the essay, “The Monuments of Passaic,” signal a shift by artists to making and showing art outside galleries — including the “exhibition” space of a mass-produced, illustrated magazine — but it also put the artist in the unusual role of writer, a position usually reserved for critics and historians. Smithson’s essay was a clever combination of genres: travelogue, science fiction and philosophical tract. But it was also a poignant meditation on time and entropy (one of his favorite terms) in postindustrial suburbia.

docs.lead_paragraph: After almost a week of previews and vernissages, today 945 Madison Avenue opened its doors for the public to descend upon the last Whitney Biennial to take place on the Upper East Side. Two years from now, the Whitney Museum of American Art will have settled into its new building beside the High Line, and the days of several hundred people in “festive attire” snaking all the way down to Park Avenue as they wait to ooh, aah and roll their eyes at the latest and greatest in ostensibly American art will be a thing of the past. In the future when the museum is at capacity, all the excess people will be pushed into the Hudson River.

docs.snippet: The unlikely host and co-host of TMC’s “The Essentials,” which begins a new season this month, discuss their shared love of film.
docs.lead_paragraph: As far as on-screen duos go, Robert Osborne and Drew Barrymore seem like an unlikely pair. He was raised in the small town of Colfax, Wash. (population 2,800) during the ’40s and amused himself with reading books while his parents worked. She grew up amidst the glitz and glamour of Hollywood in the ’80s, the youngest in a long family line of legendary actors, and made her first television appearance before she was even a year old. But they share an almost obsessive love for movies, particularly black-and-white films made decades ago. It’s this connection that makes Osborne and Barrymore light up together as the host and co-host, respectively, of TCM’s “The Essentials.” The show, which premiered in 2001 and airs on Saturday nights, puts timeless, classic films in the spotlight with commentary and fun bits of trivia supplied by the hosts (in the past those duties have been taken up by everyone from Rob Reiner to Alec Baldwin). This season marks Barrymore’s third as Osborne’s wingwoman, and the two clearly enjoy the back-and-forth banter — as well as the goofy handshakes, thumb wars and screwball comedy moments that often happen after the cameras stop rolling. T caught up with the actors on set to talk about the films that forever changed them, the characters they’ve admired and crushed on, and what’s missing from the box office today.

headline.main: Drew Barrymore and Robert Osborne on Classic Movies

docs.abstract: In the spring 2014 men’s fashion issue, T looks at the changing face of masculinity.
docs.snippet: In the spring 2014 men’s fashion issue, T looks at the changing face of masculinity.
docs.lead_paragraph: T’s spring men’s fashion issue looks at the changing face of masculinity in 2014. On the cover is the chameleonic actor Benedict Cumberbatch, whose unconventional looks, unassuming personality and ability to embody any role (he got his start playing women’s parts in Shakespeare) have made him an unlikely megastar. We visit estates in Austria and Ireland, where, respectively, the mischievous sculptor Erwin Wurm and the reclusive novelist J.P. Donleavy are living out their idiosyncratic visions. We also dive into the supersize life of the boxing champ Floyd Mayweather Jr., whose taste for excess and bold proclamations are a throwback to the days of Muhammad Ali. And we round things out with a group of men unafraid to share their passions and opinions: Gary Shteyngart and CeeLo Green, who consider Justin Bieber socks and bathe with beer soap; the writer Troy Patterson, who waxes poetic about the many meanings of man bags; and the designer Dries Van Noten, whose original collage lays bare the inspirations that have shaped his 30-year career. See all stories from the issue >>

docs.lead_paragraph: Samuel Kingston, a Union soldier and prisoner of war, languished in a dungeon on a late winter’s day in March 1864. The cell was in the basement of infamous Libby Prison in Richmond, Va., the capital of the Confederacy. A severe cough and cold racked his body. His cellmates were similarly affected. Ten in all, they were crammed into a dank, drafty cell not much larger than a common tent. Rebel guards provided Kingston and the others with nothing more than scraps of food for subsistence and an open bucket for a toilet. If some of the guards had had their way, the prisoners would be left to rot in the filth and cold of the converted brick warehouse.

docs.abstract: Comments on my Sunday column about domestic violence and how to curb it.
docs.snippet: Comments on my Sunday column about domestic violence and how to curb it.
docs.lead_paragraph: When I lecture about our book “Half the Sky,” which focuses on women’s rights in the rest of the world, I’m always asked about gender issues here in the United States. And I answer that the two most serious issues are probably two that don’t get as much attention as they should: domestic violence and human trafficking. Today my column is about domestic violence, but it’s something that we in the news business don’t cover enough–considering that it strikes one American woman in four, and a higher share of women worldwide. It’s a complicated issue, but it’s also one where I think we have the tools to do much, much better. Police are attentive in some jurisdictions, but not nearly enough in others, and that’s a crucial step to reduce the toll.

headline.main: Readers Commenting on Domestic Violence

docs.lead_paragraph: Fox announced that it had renewed four shows for next season: one drama, “The Following,” and three comedies, “New Girl,” “Brooklyn Nine-Nine” and “The Mindy Project.” The ratings for “Brooklyn Nine-Nine” have been low — its last four episodes averaged only 2.8 million total viewers — but the show won two Golden Globes in January, for best comedy and best leading comedy actor (Andy Samberg). “The Following” and “New Girl” have also struggled when judged by traditional ratings of viewers who watch programs live, but both shows continue to rank among the best in broadcast programming when including viewers in the 18- to 49-year-old demographic who watch using DVRs. The renewal for “The Mindy Project” is more of a surprise. This season it has averaged 2.6 million total viewers, and it is now on a two-month hiatus. It is scheduled to return with new episodes on April 1.

docs.lead_paragraph: In 2007, a droll, bespectacled black man with fluttery hand gestures named Stew turned the New York theater world on its head with “Passing Strange,” his big, raucous rock musical about an arty African-American who finds sexual and artistic freedom in the cafes and art collectives of Amsterdam and Berlin. That may sound like an esoteric envelope for a musical, but Stew, alongside a terrific team of writers and performers, pulled it off with a cycle of open-hearted pop-rock showstoppers, as if James Baldwin had partnered with the Who. Since “Passing Strange,” Stew has mostly played new numbers at small Brooklyn venues like Barbès. But this weekend, he took his “New Stew Review,” featuring a large and exuberant retinue of musicians and guest singers, to the posh 54 Below in Midtown. The staid setting in no way stopped Stew from serving up his special sauce of astute lyrics, gorgeous melodies and funky grooves that nearly lifted the supper-club audience out of its seats.

docs.abstract: Every two weeks, T exclusively presents a new installation from the artist’s video series entitled “Things I’m (Probably) Not Going to Get Done for the Biennial.”
docs.snippet: Every two weeks, T exclusively presents a new installation from the artist’s video series entitled “Things I’m (Probably) Not Going to Get Done for the Biennial.”
docs.lead_paragraph: Nearly three months ago, Darren Bader approached T in the hope that we’d host his off-site video contribution to this year’s Whitney Biennial. The plan, he explained, was to post a series of fake news stories on our website — without attributing them to him or the Whitney, and without even a wink to suggest that something funny was afoot. This idea got shut down. But there were plenty of others. The New York-based artist wanted to produce an editorial that paired celebrities with everyday objects, which echoed a show he staged in Los Angeles last summer at Blum & Poe. “Bryan Cranston and sleeping bag,” was one suggested match. “Patricia Arquette with weather balloon.” Another thought was to photograph things that rhyme, such as boule and stool, or the occult Baal and the actor Nick Stahl. In the end, time and budget constraints forced him to shelve (twelve, helve — the game gets inside you) his original slate of ideas, but Bader made the most of a trying situation. What follows is the first video from his new series, “Things I’m (Probably) Not Going to Get Done for the Biennial.” About the videos, which will run here exclusively through the duration of the Biennial, Bader has this to say: “I have ideas. You have ideas. Maybe some of them are the same.” More likely than not, this last part is untrue.

headline.main: Art Matters | Darren Bader’s Video Contribution to the 2014 Whitney Biennial

docs.lead_paragraph: Gov. Earl Ray Tomblin said he was concerned about the constitutionality of a bill banning abortions after 20 weeks of pregnancy, which the State Legislature passed over the weekend. Twelve states have passed similar bans, according to the Guttmacher Institute. But West Virginia will be the first with a Democratic governor and Democratic-controlled legislature to embrace the 20-week limit if the governor signs the bill. Supporters contend a fetus that age can feel pain, although the American Congress of Obstetricians and Gynecologists says there is no scientific evidence for that view. The Supreme Court in January refused to hear an appeal of a lower court’s decision to strike down an Arizona law banning most abortions after 20 weeks. In Roe v. Wade in 1973, the high court said women have a right to an abortion until the point of fetal viability, generally seen as 24 weeks. “The abortion bill obviously is one that causes me some concern because even the legislative attorneys and others said they feel this bill is unconstitutional,” Governor Tomblin said in a statement.

docs.lead_paragraph: When I was a child, my family spent several summers in Amsterdam. My mother, sister and I toured the city, wandered along the canals, visited the great museums and sampled the local chocolates. My father, meanwhile, buried himself in Amsterdam’s social history library, studying the papers of the anarchists Emma Goldman and Alexander Berkman, known as Sasha. Sasha and Emma had been born in czarist Russia, immigrated to New York in the 1880s as teenagers, joined an anarchist group, and formed a lifelong friendship that remained immutable through protest rallies, bombing plots, prison time, love affairs, deportation, separation and war. My father, Paul Avrich, had been fascinated with them for years.

docs.abstract: India’s Supreme Court on Monday ordered lower courts to conclude the trials of lawmakers charged with grave crimes within a year of the date of the charges being filed as a way to reduce the number of politicians who are re-elected during drawn-out trials.
docs.snippet: India’s Supreme Court on Monday ordered lower courts to conclude the trials of lawmakers charged with grave crimes within a year of the date of the charges being filed as a way to reduce the number of politicians who are re-elected during drawn-ou...
docs.lead_paragraph: India’s Supreme Court on Monday ordered lower courts to conclude the trials of lawmakers charged with grave crimes within a year of the date of the charges being filed as a way to reduce the number of politicians who are re-elected during drawn-out trials. Criminal cases in India often drag on for several years, allowing lawmakers who are charged with crimes to continue to hold their posts and run for re-election. Monday’s ruling is part of a push for electoral overhaul in India. In July, the Supreme Court barred people convicted of crimes carrying prison terms of more than five years from running in elections. On Monday, it ruled that lawmakers who are charged with crimes carrying a punishment of more than two years must have a speedy trial. The Association for Democratic Reforms, a nonprofit group that aims to promote electoral transparency, estimates that 30 percent of sitting lawmakers have criminal charges against them.

headline.main: India’s Supreme Court Orders Speedier Trials for Lawmakers

docs.lead_paragraph: An Istanbul court on Monday ordered the release of 19 men convicted with scores of others of plotting a coup in the controversial Ergenekon case, which the government of Prime Minister Recep Tayyip Erdogan used to break the political power of Turkey’s military. The court said the men should be released because the Parliament recently reduced the maximum detention period before a conviction to five years, and the prisoners had already been detained longer than that. The court order followed the release of a former army chief last week after the Constitutional Court’s ruling critical of the conduct of the recently abolished Special Court that carried out the Ergenekon trial. The trial, which lasted five years, prompted criticism at home and abroad, with several international organizations describing the prosecution of the more than 200 suspects as unfair, with unnecessary arrests, secret witnesses and disputes over evidence. Some Turkish analysts characterized Monday’s releases as part of a bid by the government to increase its popularity before local elections in two weeks and gain the upper hand in a power struggle with a pro-Islamic network influential in the judiciary and the police.

headline.main: Turkish Court Orders Release of 19 More in Plot Case

docs.lead_paragraph: MIMICRY IS AN ART FORM in processed foods, and the makers of Oreo cookies have outdone themselves with their latest attempt to jazz up their icon: the Cookie Dough Oreo. The fun in dissecting this marvel of food engineering begins right on the front of the package, which sports pictures of real-looking cookie dough and chocolate chips, though neither is found inside. Instead, this newest version of the Oreo draws on a mix of extra sugar, precision chemistry and a marketing maneuver that industry insiders call “permission” to evoke the mere impression of cookie dough. Its success may be measured less in sales than in the buzz it generates for the Oreo line.

docs.lead_paragraph: The Food and Drug Administration on Tuesday said it had approved the first medical device to prevent migraine headaches. The device, made by a Belgian company, Cephaly Technology, is small, portable and battery powered, and it looks like a plastic headband. It is worn across the forehead and over the ears, and contains a small electrode that applies an electric current to stimulate the nerve that is associated with migraine headaches. A study of 67 people in Belgium found that those who used the device reported significantly fewer days with migraines per month than those who used a placebo.

headline.main: F.D.A. Approves Anti-Migraine Device

docs.lead_paragraph: President Obama on Tuesday moved to preserve more than 1,600 acres of coastal land in Northern California by declaring them part of a national monument. Point Arena-Stornetta, a 12-mile stretch of coast made up of federal and state public lands, is about 140 miles north of San Francisco. It will now be part of the California Coastal National Monument, a marine boundary that includes islands, rocks and reefs owned by the United States and within 12 miles of California’s 1,100-mile coast. Point Arena-Stornetta is the first shoreline portion of the monument. “It is a place where scientists do research; where people who just want to experience the great outdoors can take advantage of it,” Mr. Obama said before signing the proclamation. The newly expanded coastal monument is home to a variety of fauna and flora, among them Steller sea lions, Behren’s silverspot butterfly, rare bird species like the black oystercatcher, and a bishop pine forest.

docs.lead_paragraph: The government is considering contracts with climbing companies that would grant exclusive access to many of its highest mountains, a spokesman for Nepal’s tourism ministry said on Tuesday, as part of an effort to bring more climbers to the Himalayas, the world’s highest mountain range. Nepal has some 3,310 mountains, but only 310 are open to commercial climbing. Since the government determined that it cannot manage all of its peaks, it will soon propose offering 30-year leases on the remaining 3,000 mountains to climbing companies, which would then organize climbs and charge fees. Nepal collects about $2.7 million annually in mountaineering fees, most of which comes from the nearly 35,000 people who visit Mount Everest. Nepal has long been trying to increase and diversify its tourism business, with its extraordinary mountains — 60 peaks higher than 26,000 feet — at the center of those efforts. Nepal is one of the world’s poorest countries, and the country’s youths are increasingly leaving for jobs elsewhere.

headline.main: Nepal: Push to Open Peaks to Climbers

docs.snippet: The multi-hyphenate sensation teams up with a pair of French designers to craft a custom ride.
docs.lead_paragraph: Pharrell Williams’s style is almost as popular as his music this year. In January, the Twittersphere buzzed when the artist arrived to the red carpet wearing a Vivienne Westwood hat that looked undeniably similar to the Arby’s logo. A week ago, social media flared up again when Williams walked into the Oscars with his hands shoved into the pockets of a pair of Lanvin tuxedo shorts. And yet somehow, the luxe limited-edition Brooklyn Bike that he created with the Paris duo Bruno Domeau and Philip Pérès and Brooklyn Machine Works — a New York-based bike company that Williams co-owns — is flying just under the trending hashtag radar. Just looking at the bright-yellow water-buffalo leather hand-stitched around its frame makes you feel as happy as Williams’s song of the same name. It’s available exclusively at Atelier Courbet, a new SoHo shop and gallery that represents artisan workshops — like the one run by Domeau and Pérès, who, before setting up shop together, were craftsmen for Hermès. The made-to-order pieces are customized for each client; at $16,500, it is more a piece of art than a way to get around town.

headline.main: A Luxe Leather Bike Designed by Pharrell
headline.print_headline: Feeling for: Big Hat Optional

docs.lead_paragraph: Few things will ruin a cruise faster than feeling seasick. To help prevent motion sickness, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends staying hydrated, curbing alcohol and caffeinated drinks, eating small meals and limiting external stimuli (closing your eyes, lying face down or keeping your eyes on the horizon). And while some experts say that cabins in the middle of the lower deck of a ship may help temper motion sickness, the C.D.C. has reported that “cabin location on a cruise ship does not appear to influence the likelihood of motion sickness.”

headline.main: Prone to Seasickness? Distraction Might Help
headline.print_headline: Prone to Seasickness? Nature’s Own Remedies

docs.lead_paragraph: For a certain type of girl during a certain stretch of the aughts, I Heart — the late, lamented subterranean NoLIta boutique housed in Sonic Youth’s former practice space — was more than a place to shop for night-out looks from under-the-radar designers; it was a second home of sorts, a spot for kicking back, listening to obscure dance records and reading ‘zines. That store’s owner, Jill Bradshaw, recently decamped to Austin, Tex., her old college stomping grounds. Now, just in time for the South by Southwest conference, she has joined forces with two more Brooklyn expats, the restaurateurs Greg Mathews and Jade Place Mathews, to open Friends & Neighbors, an equally convivial concept store housed in a residential bungalow in burgeoning East Austin.

docs.snippet: In “Leaving China,” the author and illustrator James McMullan writes about his childhood in China, India, Canada and the United States.
docs.lead_paragraph: Lush violet shadows, a sense of the page as a deep box — a stage, really — in which a quiet drama unfolds in acute perspective: New Yorkers may recognize James McMullan’s signature watercolors from his posters for Lincoln Center Theater. (His saucy sailor girl, looking back over her shoulder to advertise a production of “Anything Goes” at the Vivian Beaumont, is a particularly well-known example.) New York Times readers may remember the illustrated 12-part series McMullan wrote on the artistic process for the Opinionator blog in 2010. And children and their art-loving parents will recall the many picture books he has illustrated, including the Times Best Illustrated winner “I Stink!” — written by his wife, Kate McMullan — a first-person account of the life of a garbage truck. “Know what I do at night while you’re asleep? Eat your trash, that’s what! See those bags? I smell breakfast!”

headline.main: A New York Artist’s Wartime Childhood

docs.lead_paragraph: Cardinal Reinhard Marx, 60, the archbishop of Munich, was selected on Wednesday to head the Roman Catholic bishops’ conference in Germany. Known as outspoken, the cardinal is a confidant of Pope Francis, who this month named him head of a new Economic Council at the Vatican. Cardinal Marx succeeds Robert Zöllitsch as the effective leader of Germany’s 24 million Roman Catholics. He is known for emphasizing the need for the church to stand by its teachings and acts, and wrote a book — called “Das Kapital,” in a dig at Karl Marx’s 19th-century treatise — that vigorously warns against the dangers of an unbridled market economy. He has also sought ways to allow Catholics who divorce and then remarry to take Communion. “We cannot treat these people as second-class Christians,” the German DPA news agency quoted him as saying.

headline.main: Germany: Bishops Select Pope’s Confidant as New Leader

docs.lead_paragraph: A year and a half ago, the French-born, Milan-based artist Nathalie Du Pasquier had never heard of American Apparel. She’s not quite as mature as Jacky O’Shaughnessy, the 62-year-old star of a recent ad campaign for the downtown-L.A.-based brand, but Du Pasquier does prefer to dress her own age (which is 57). Beginning today, though, Du Pasquier’s signature colorful, graphic patterns will grace the 20 newest silhouettes hanging in a select 20 of the label’s many retail outposts. The collaboration came about when the brand’s creative director, Iris Alonzo, approached Du Pasquier about painting prints similar to the iconic ones she produced in the 1980s as an original member of the Memphis Group, the Milan-based collective of designers and architects. “I thought, Why not?” Du Pasquier remembers. “It was the first collaboration with a fashion company in many, many years actually because I am a painter. I have not done that kind of work in a long time.” And how does the artist feel about American Apparel now that it’s emblazoned with work from her own hand? “These?” she asks about the simple frocks, jumpsuits and skirts, minimalist shapes that complement her bright, unruly designs. “I will wear them, yes.” There are shirts for men, too, and more cheerful accessories from the capsule will roll out during the summer months to come.

headline.main: A Memphis Group Founder Creates Prints for American Apparel

docs.abstract: I can live with the joy of new motherhood without losing the memory of loving my son for his three short years or the daily painful reminder that I will never see or hold him again.
docs.snippet: I can live with the joy of new motherhood without losing the memory of loving my son for his three short years or the daily painful reminder that I will never see or hold him again.
docs.lead_paragraph: On a cold night in February 2013, my son Ronan died of Tay-Sachs disease. He was nearly 3 years old. During the course of his life he experienced seizures, lost his sight and volitional movement, and finally, his ability to eat. From the time of his diagnosis at 9 months old — the worst day of my life; the day that drew a line between the person I was before I knew he was sick and the person I am now after his death — my ideas about parenting shifted irreversibly. I cast off all notions of what the future might hold for Ronan. I accepted, however reluctantly, that my task was not to prepare my son for his future, but to make each day and each moment count until the day of his death.

headline.main: ‘Dragon Mother’ Emily Rapp: A New Baby Doesn’t, and Shouldn’t, Replace What’s Lost

docs.lead_paragraph: Bill Cunningham calls himself a street photographer, and in a way he is the innovator and prototype of that calling. Mr. Cunningham is modest and reserved, and street photographer doesn’t fully explain his practice. He isn’t a street photographer in the same sense as Elliott Erwitt or Gary Winogrand. He is not looking for extraordinary happenstance to make a remarkable picture; he is on the street to document the passing parade of fashion where it really lives — and as the public wears it, not as it is presented by editors, stylists and fashion photographers. As Mr. Cunningham has put it, “The fashion show has always just been on the street.”

In Bellow’s parody, Bellow, Malamud and Roth were the literary equivalent of the much advertised men’s wear company — but lighthearted as it was, the joke cut two ways: it was a declaration of imagination’s independence of collective tailoring, and it laughingly struck out at the disgruntlement of those who, having themselves applied the label in pique, felt displaced by it.

We appreciate this immensely: it’s free, we trust her, the boys adore her and she seems to enjoy it. The problem is, she leaves our house a mess. docs.lead_paragraph: For a guy who often plays nice, Jason Bateman sure knows how to wrap his lips around invective. He doesn’t have an especially rubbery mouth, the kind that Jerry Lewis could stretch until it almost snapped, nor does it curl with the puckered elasticity displayed in the poster for “Bad Words,” a comedy about a guy who crashes children’s spelling bees. Sometimes, he just opens wide, and out pops an expletive. At other times, he turns his nice-guy face toward the target, pauses for a beat or two while he sizes up the opposition — maybe sends out a decoy, like a faint smile or a deceptively inviting word — and then he slashes and burns. The kids take it hard.

docs.snippet: In “Enemy,” directed by Denis Villeneuve, Jake Gyllenhaal plays a history professor who sees his double and starts stalking him.
docs.lead_paragraph: The double is an ancient and irresistible literary theme, especially beloved by philosophically minded scaremongers like Edgar Allan Poe, whose tale “William Wilson” is a concise classic on the matter. The idea of a second self — who might be the manifestation of madness, an allegory come to life or the result of a supernatural glitch in the order of things — is both frightening and fascinating. Movies make the conceit literal with the simple trick of using the same actor in two roles. Who can forget the two Kim Novaks driving James Stewart around the bend in “Vertigo”?

docs.abstract: As bottles sealed with cork became more common, corkscrews did too.
docs.snippet: As bottles sealed with cork became more common, corkscrews did too.
docs.lead_paragraph: For as long as wine was stored in jugs and stoppered with oil cloth and bits of wood, there was no need for a specialized opener. But in the 17th century, as bottles sealed with cork became more common, corkscrews did too. Collectors say that very early versions of the tool were derived from military kits: Soldiers used screw-shaped “gun worms” to pull misfired musket balls from the barrels of their guns. They would drill into the lead and drag the ammunition up and out. The first corkscrews were small and portable, often nothing more than the worm (the screw itself) and a small ring for pulling with your finger. But in the 18th century, people came to understand the benefits of aging wine, and bottles were standardized in a long-necked cylindrical shape suitable for long-term storage. The new emphasis on shelf life necessitated a better cork — and thus a better corkscrew.

headline.main: Who Made That Corkscrew?

Its characters are stock types or caricatures, and its descriptions, sketchy for prose, are almost mock-poetry (“the pitiless turbine / of his thoughts”). docs.lead_paragraph: Any novelist who’s ever stood in a bookstore, watching as someone picks up a copy of her book and pauses before returning it to the shelf, knows there’s no logical explanation for why particular books appeal to particular people. Over time, though, readers do tend to make intuitive decisions. Someone who wants a fast-moving story may seek out what she imagines is a plot-driven novel. Someone who wants to spend time in close quarters, getting to know a person like herself, or perhaps like no one she’s ever met, may choose what appears to be a character-­driven novel. docs.lead_paragraph: “Wow . . . New York! Just like I pictured it. Skyscrapers and everything.” So murmurs a presumably wide-eyed newcomer during a spoken-word break in Stevie Wonder’s “Living for the City,” and who among us outlanders and former rubes did not feel that same sense of mingled recognition and awe when we first set foot here? Thanks to movies and TV, magazines, the news, books — iconography in general — all of us, even natives, carry a mental suitcase stuffed with received images of the Big Apple. That’s true of children, too, for whom the city’s superlatives (biggest, loudest, tallest) hold a special fascination. You might even say that New York is to other American cities what dinosaurs are to other animals — minus, one hopes, the extinction event. And if we are — or were — lucky children, picture books play a huge role in how we picture the city, from “Eloise” and “The Snowy Day” to “Lyle, Lyle, Crocodile,” “In the Night Kitchen,” “You Can’t Take a Balloon Into the Metropolitan Museum” and “The Man Who Walked Between the Towers.”

docs.lead_paragraph: Top Cat: The great independent publisher New Directions has been around since 1936, offering a home to authors including William Carlos Williams, Muriel Spark and Roberto Bolaño. But it didn’t land its first New York Times best seller until last month, when Takashi Hiraide’s novel “The Guest Cat” — a sweet philosophical story (translated from Japanese) about a jaded couple who embrace life again after a neighbor’s cat adopts them — briefly surfaced on the trade paperback list. “It took everyone fantastically by surprise here,” Michael Barron, the publicity director for New Directions, said via email. “We didn’t think it would do this well. . . . Only a few people seemed interested in reviewing it, but one of those was Juan Vidal, a reviewer for NPR Books. His rave review is a testament to the power of social media — it was posted by NPR Books, and then reposted by the main NPR site, which has over a million followers. It got thousands of likes on Facebook, and was heavily retweeted. That same day it was picked up by NPR, we watched as ‘The Guest Cat’ climbed up and up the Amazon sales list to the top 20 sellers. But the big news was when it hit the New York Times best-seller list, our first book ever to do so, and all because of a single review.”

docs.lead_paragraph: On the first full evening of last month’s second annual Steampunk cruise to the Bahamas, I found myself — in tuxedo and a World War I-era aviator’s cap — marching in a strange parade past the Deck 5 duty-free shops on the Royal Caribbean cruise ship  Explorer of the Seas. Strolling with me were 62 elaborately costumed Victorian re-enactors, including but not restricted to: a Gypsy minstrel playing the accordion, a princess in authentic Turkoman beads, a Russian submarine commander, an African explorer in safari gear, some mustached gentlemen in John Bull top hats and, in her tiara, a 60-year-old woman dressed up as Her Majesty the Queen.

headline.main: Steampunks at Sea

docs.lead_paragraph: The radiant sun was starting its late-afternoon descent, leaving behind pleasantly warm air, and I was gliding on glassy water through a Gambian archipelago of tropical rain-forest islands in a brightly painted boat, a converted ferry with an upper deck and even a soft-drink bar. Propped against pillows with my feet up, I was as comfortable as Cleopatra on her royal barge. Suddenly, Assan, our guide, spotted our goal: a big, black chimpanzee sitting on the wet, brown shoreline, eating fruit. And then there was another one, with a baby chimp swinging from its belly, high up in the trees.
